metas.name: Agriculture - Breeding
metas.note: It is not so rare to see cows, horses, or sheep in France in Geoguessr. If that ever happens, you should consider the West of the country (Brittany, Normandy), as well as the mountainous regions (Pyrenees and Alps). This is where you have the most chances to find animals in France in Google Street View.
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Agriculture - Corn
metas.note: Corn fields are mostly located in the Western part of the country, as well as in some areas in the East of Paris, and around Lyon and Strasbourg.
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Agriculture - Lavender Fields
metas.note: Lavender fields can be found in the southeast, appearing as small grey bushes when not fully grown.

metas.name: Agriculture - Salt Farms
metas.note: Salt farms, which appear as flooded trenches with grass medians, are unique to the west coastal islands of Île de Ré and Île d'Oléron as well as the nearby coast (especially Guerande), as well as some very niche areas in the South of France (Camargue).
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt & France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Agriculture - Sunflower
metas.note: Sunflowers are mostly found in the southwest of the country, particularly around Toulouse.

metas.name: Agriculture - Wine
metas.note: France is the second largest wine producer in the world, with many famed wine regions. The most common include the area around Bordeaux, southern coast and Champagne, East of Paris. Other regions include, but are not limited to, Loire Valley, Alsace and Corsica.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt & France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Architecture - Alpine Architecture
metas.note:
Alpine architecture, unmistakable for its light coloured base and extensive wooden elements, is unsurprisingly found in the Alps.

NOTE: Similar houses can be found in the touristic parts of Pyrenees.

metas.name: Architecture - Basque Architecture
metas.note:
White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area. The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.

NOTE: They’re also common in parts of Northern Spain, where the timber frames are usually unpainted.

metas.name: Architecture - Belle-Île-en-Mer Architecture
metas.note:
On the Breton island Belle-Île-en-Mer you can find houses typical for Brittany combined with colourful façades and outlines, superficially similar to houses in Portugal.

NOTE: The entire island was only covered with an often oversaturated Generation 2 camera.

metas.name: Architecture - Black Shingle Roof
metas.note: Black shingle roofs are primarily found in the northwest, the rough cutoff being the Loire river. Other areas include near the Belgian border, the south-centre, and the Pyrenees, making black roofs a good clue for Alps-Pyrenees toss-ups.

metas.name: Architecture - Black Shingle Roofs with Mountains
metas.note: Black shingle roofs are often found in the Pyrenees, making black roofs a good clue for Alps-Pyrenees toss-ups.

metas.name: Architecture - Brick House / Black Roof
metas.note:
Found in the North (mostly Belgium border)

Note by MB: Brick Houses also often have Red Roofs. Houses with Black Roofs do not appear around Toulouse (unlike those with red roofs).

What I find more useful to differentiate the roof types is the materials. "Black Roofs" are shingles, while "Red Roofs" are actual tiles (which can also get very dark)
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Architecture - Brick House / Red Rooftiles
metas.note:
Brick roofs with red rooftiles can be found in the North mostly. Sometimes, they're also found around Toulouse.

Note by MB: With red tiles, Toulouse is an option, with black shingles, it isn't. What I find more useful to differentiate the roof types is the materials. "Black Roofs" are shingles, while "Red Roofs" are actual tiles (which can also get very dark)
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Architecture - Brittany Architecture
metas.note: Brittany has one of the most recognizable and consistent architectures in the country. Common elements include, in addition to black roofs, edge chimneys, black slate walls and stones surrounding doors and windows. The walls will be either very light coloured or made of stone.

metas.name: Architecture - Germanic Architecture
metas.note:
Many elements of Germanic architecture are concentrated in Alsace, such as timber framing and half-hip roof. Furthermore, roofs with fish scale tiles are more common in this region.

Beware that these elements are sometimes incorporated into architecture in other parts of France, and are most reliable in conjunction with one another.

metas.name: Architecture - Ile de France Architecture
metas.note: Walls made of uneven cream coloured to orange stones, glued with mortar and often incorporating red brick details can be found in the towns surrounding Paris. Note that the city of Paris itself generally does not have this architecture.

metas.name: Architecture - Mansard Roof
metas.note:
Mansard roofs, also known as French windows, are a very common feature of Parisian architecture. They’re made up of steep black shingle roofs with inserted dormer windows. While not unique to Paris, it is a good clue in abundance and on wide boulevards.

On some occasions, they can also be found in the North of France.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt & France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Architecture - Old Toulouse Architecture
metas.note: In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find bright orange brick buildings. They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as wooden shutters, being common.

metas.name: Architecture - Stone House / Black Shingle Roof
metas.note:
Found in Western France, mainly in Bretagne.

Note by MB: What I find more useful to differentiate the roof types is the materials. "Black Roofs" are shingles, while "Red Roofs" are actual tiles (which can also get very dark)
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Architecture - Stone House / Red Rooftiles
metas.note:
Can be found all over France, but mainly central and southern.

Note by MB: What I find more useful to differentiate the roof types is the materials. "Black Roofs" are shingles, while "Red Roofs" are actual tiles (which can also get very dark)
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Architecture - U-Tiles
metas.note: Roofs in the south of the country will often be made up of rounded tiles overlapping one another, often varying in colour.

metas.name: Architecture - West Coast Architecture
metas.note: The houses along the West Coast, from Nantes to Bayonne are usually low, with white walls, and red roofs.
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Car Meta - Rare Antenna - Black & White
metas.note:
On rare occasions, you may find a flag attached to the antenna in the generation 3 coverage. While much of the highlighted areas has been overwritten, learning the distribution of each antenna can yield very high scores.

The black/white flag can be found in Calvados, Orne, Eastern Bourgogne and Loire/Haut de Loire

metas.name: Car Meta - Rare Antenna - Blue
metas.note:
On rare occasions, you may find a flag attached to the antenna in the generation 3 coverage. While much of the highlighted areas has been overwritten, learning the distribution of each antenna can yield very high scores.

The blue flag can be found in Bas-Rhin, Aube and the Correze/Haute-Vienne/Dordogne Tristate

metas.name: Car Meta - Rare Antenna - Red
metas.note:
On rare occasions, you may find a flag attached to the antenna in the generation 3 coverage. While much of the highlighted areas has been overwritten, learning the distribution of each antenna can yield very high scores.

The red flag can be found in the eastern part of the Nord-Department

metas.name: Infrastructure - Azure Blue Signpost
metas.note:
On the French Riviera (Côte d'Azur in French, literally translated as Blue Coast), you can find regular traffic signposts painted azure blue. Uniquely, Cagnes-sur-mer, west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.

NOTE: Blue infrastructure can be found to a lesser extent all across France, particularly Brittany, so consider the landscape as well.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Bordeaux Signpost
metas.note:
In the outskirts of Bordeaux, you may find square traffic signposts with the Bordeaux shade of red, named after the wine grown in the region.

NOTE: Red posts by themselves are not unique to Bordeaux, so apply this meta with caution.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Bordeaux Streetsign
metas.note: Small tables with 'Arrᵗ' written on a small separate sign, are found in Bordeaux, despite being a city not divided into arrondissements.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Brown Signback
metas.note:
Road signs where both the post and back are painted brown are most commonly found in Seine-et-Marne, and rarely in Ille-et-Vilaine. It is more reliable when the post is square, however round signposts are equally common.

NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Cityname Roadsign
metas.note:
Street signs in the metropolitan area of Paris often say the name of the city, which is generally atypical for street signs in France. The signs will often be made in a modern design, and many city names will be river based, notably named after Seine and Marne.

NOTE: This can be seen sporadically throughout the country, so consider other clues.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Cuboid Barrier
metas.note:
Cuboid barriers made of stones and mortar are commonly found on Corsica. While by no means unique to Corsica, it is good to consider the island when you see them in rounds with a plausible Mediterranean landscape.

NOTE: Stone barriers with a rounded top are not found on Corsica.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Dark Green Signpost
metas.note:
Dark green road signposts and backs are most commonly found in Brittany and around Paris, but also various southern regions in the country.

NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Eure-et-Loir Sticker
metas.note: Signbacks in Eure-et-Loir may include a green sticker, the department’s logo. They’re usually placed on a dark green back, without a matching post.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Grey Signback / Green Signpost
metas.note:
A greyish green signback supported by a darker green post, is found in three areas: Brittany (Côtes-d'Armor and eastern half of Ille-et-Vilaine), Pyrénées-Atlantiques and rarely near the Alps.

NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Lille Streetsign
metas.note: Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Lyon Streetsign
metas.note:
Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an uninterrupted inner white border that cuts a notch for the arrondissement and each bolt.

NOTE: Outside Lyon proper, the street sign will display the name of the suburb instead.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Marseille Streetsign
metas.note: Marseille’s street signs will usually feature the city’s emblem, a variation of the Greek cross. The white border will usually be interrupted at the top, even when the cross is absent.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Montpellier Streetsign
metas.note: Montpellier street signs will typically contain a blue ‘M’ on a white background in the top left corner.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Paris Streetsign
metas.note:
Paris uses an iconic green & Prussian blue design with a top arch that has also been replicated in Bucharest, which is sometimes referred to as Paris of the east.

NOTE: The simple rectangular form of the sign can be found in the towns nearby and rarely in other cities.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Pas-de-Calais Sign
metas.note:
In the Pas-de-Calais department, you may find road signs with the following colour arrangement: a dark green post paired with a signback of a lighter shade of green, ranging from matcha green to greenish turquoise. The department’s logo, a green and blue triangle, is occasionally present on the signback.

NOTE: Under certain lighting, they can appear similar to the greyish road signs. Also, beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Powder Blue Infrastructure
metas.note: Uniquely, Cagnes-sur-mer, west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Reddish Road
metas.note:
Roads with a significant red, purple or burgundy tint are most commonly found in an area between Paris and Dijon, with Normandy being a notable exception. The historical region of Burgundy, which gave the name to the shade of red, roughly corresponds to the highlighted area.

NOTE: Normal roads may deceptively look reddish under some lighting, so use this with caution.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Thin B-Type Guardrail
metas.note:
Thin B type guardrail, typical for Czechia and Slovakia, is sometimes found on highways in the northern half of the country, often coming from Le Mans, Tours, Paris, Reims and Metz.

NOTE: On the highlighted sections, thin B can be the minority guardrail, and short sections of any highway will have no guardrails at all. It is also more common on smaller roads in the North, but less consistent as a clue.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Wind Turbine
metas.note: Wind turbines are considerably more common in the north of the country.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Front License Plates
metas.note: France can sometimes have yellow back license plates, especially in old coverage. Should you see several yellow plates on the front, you're probably near Luxembourg.

metas.name: Landscape - British Hedges
metas.note:
Rural roads surrounded by hedges blocking the view, reminiscent of the British Isles, are primarily found in the northwest, particularly in Normandy.

NOTE: Hedges by themselves are not sufficient for recognizing this area and are common all over France.

metas.name: Landscape - Cote d'Azur
metas.note: The French Riviera (Cote d'Azur) will mirror many characteristics of Monaco. Rich areas with planted palms and light coloured multi story buildings with wide balconies are good indications you’re in this area, with the rest of the southern coast and Corsican Bastia sharing similar vibes.

metas.name: Landscape - La Beauce
metas.note:
La Beauce is one of the flattest regions of France, located South of Paris.

Apart from the flatness of the area, the important thing to notice about the fields in the Beauce region is that they are industrialized. You will not see hedges around the fields like you could see in the West of France. So, if you see very flat and industrialized fields with potatoes or cereals, you can be in this area. Still, the Paris hedge remains good because there are many fields North and East of Paris (but you will never get a 5K by guessing Paris out of fields).
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Landscape - Mountains
metas.note: The tallest mountains are found in the southeast and on the Spanish border.

metas.name: Language - Alsatian
metas.note: Alsatian, a dialect of German, is occasionally found in Alsace, a region that changed countries 4 times in modern history. Most bilingual street signs use some variation of gasse or strasse.

metas.name: Language - Basque
metas.note:
Bilingual signs in Basque, a language isolate, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a thinner font, which is unique within all minority languages in France.

The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.

metas.name: Language - Breton
metas.note: Breton is a Celtic language, visually most similar to Welsh. Common letters include d, k, w and the letter ñ, which is not found in French. It is commonly found on the Breton peninsula, with bilingual street signs as east as Rennes and rarely Nantes. The Breton word for street is straed.

metas.name: Language - Catalan
metas.note:
The far southern department Pyrénées-Orientales, also known as Catalunya Nord (Northern Catalonia), uses Catalan on their various signage.

It is closely related to both Spanish and French, with Ç being considerably more common than in French. The word for street is carrer.

metas.name: Language - Corsican
metas.note: On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in Corsican, a Romance language that utilises many features found in Italian, like words almost always ending in vowels. In particular, the endings u/iu/ju, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican. Moreover, placenames will usually have an Italian origin.

metas.name: Language - German Roadnames
metas.note: Streets containing German names are concentrated in Alsace.

metas.name: Language - Occitan
metas.note: Occitan is a Romance language closely related to Catalan that’s sparsely concentrated in the South of France, most often found on street signs in big cities, and very rarely on town entry signs. It can be divided into dialects, each using a slightly different word for street, all similar to Catalan “carrer”. For example, in Toulouse, you’ll find the Languedocian carrièra and in Avignon carriero, in the Provençal dialect

metas.name: Language - Occitan - Carriera
metas.note: Different dialects of Occitan use different words for 'road'. Carriera can be found in South Central France.

metas.name: Language - Occitan - Carriero
metas.note: Different dialects of Occitan use different words for 'road'. Carriero can be found in South-Eastern Coastal France.

metas.name: Language - Plou- Prefix
metas.note: Towns with the Plou- prefix are concentrated in Northwestern Brittany.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -ac
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -ac can be found in the Southwestern Quarter of France and in Brittany.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -ach
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -ach can be found in Alsace.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -anjou
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -anjou can be found in Maine-et-Loire.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -as
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -as can be found in the Southern half of France.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -at
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -at can be found in the Central South of France.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -ay
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -ay can be found in the Northern half of France.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -bearn
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -bearn can be found in Pyrenees Atlantique.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -beauce
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -beauce can be found between Essone and Vendome.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -bresse
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -bresse can be found on the border between Jura and Saone-et-Loire.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -brie
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -brie can be found in Seine-Et-Marne

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -caux
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -caux can be found in Seine-Maritime

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -court
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -court can be found in Hauts-de-France and Grand-Est

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -ey
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -ey can be found on the eastern border, in Normandy and in the Southwest.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -heim
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -heim can be found in Alsace.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -iller
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -iller can be found in Alsace.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -quercy
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -quercy can be found in Lot and Tarn-et-Garonne

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -touraine
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -touraine can be found in Indre-et-Loire.

metas.name: Language - Town Suffix: -ville
metas.note: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -ville can be found in Grand-Est and Normandy, and sometimes in between.

metas.name: Language - Water Town Name
metas.note:
Many French cities contain the name of the river they lay on, usually in the format -sur-[river]. On signage, sur are often shortened to ˢ/, in this case Chalonnes-sur-Loire (Chalonnes upon Loire). The picture shows five of the longest and therefore most common origins of river based names, but cities can bear the name of any river, regardless of length.

Similarly, city names containing -sur-mer (=on sea) or -plage (=beach) are found exclusively on the coast.

metas.name: Trekker - Boat Trekker
metas.note: Several cities along the Cote d'Azur host boat trekkers in their harbours.

metas.name: Vegetation - Maritime Pine Forest
metas.note: Forests made up entirely of Maritime pines (pinus pinaster) are found in the southwest of the country (Gironde and Landes departments). The whole area will be fairly flat, which is not typical of other areas with such pines.

metas.name: Vegetation - Meditteranean Vegetation
metas.note:
The vegetation near the South-East coast looks very Mediterranean.

Note by MB: This is more of a vibe thing tbh.
metas.footer: Source: France Tips for Geoguessr by Guigz

metas.name: Vegetation - Stone Pine
metas.note: Stone pines are commonly found along the southern coast, often planted alongside urban roads. You may however find them as north as Nantes.
